elements.element: Customer has no exclusivity or sole-supplier obligation.
elements.evidence: Revised Section 2.2 reads: "Vendor will be a non-exclusive provider of hosted analytics services, and Customer has no exclusivity or sole-supplier obligation." The original "sole and exclusive provider ... throughout the term" language is gone; Section 2.1 (no minimum or purchase commitment) and Section 12.3 (Vendor acknowledges no exclusivity commitment) are consistent, so no requirements or sole-supply obligation on Customer survives anywhere.

elements.element: Exclusivity is limited to a defined product category.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: the redline eliminates exclusivity entirely (Vendor is expressly a "non-exclusive provider"), so there is no exclusivity to confine to a product category. The vacuous satisfaction is more favourable to Customer than the fallback.

elements.element: Exclusivity lasts no longer than 12 months.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: no exclusivity period exists after the edit; the full-term exclusive dealing sentence has been replaced with a non-exclusive appointment.

elements.element: Exclusivity ends automatically if Vendor fails to meet service levels.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: with no exclusivity obligation on Customer, no performance-based exit is needed; Section 12.3 confirms Customer may engage any supplier at any time.

elements.element: Exclusivity ends automatically if Vendor fails to meet delivery dates.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: no exclusivity commitment remains that could require a delivery-failure termination trigger.

reasons: Preferred level is complete: the operative sentence both converts the appointment to non-exclusive and states affirmatively that Customer has no exclusivity or sole-supplier obligation, which is the sole preferred element.

Fallback elements are vacuously satisfied because the redline removes exclusivity altogether; the narrowed-exclusivity structure is offered only in the margin comment as a negotiating fallback, which is appropriate and does not affect the operative text.

Minimality holds: only the offending sentence in the first Section 2.2 was touched. The added clause "and Customer has no exclusivity or sole-supplier obligation" is the element language itself rather than an extra; it mildly echoes the Section 12.3 acknowledgment but does not create an inconsistent or competing operative term. If the drafter wanted the leanest possible edit, "Vendor will be a non-exclusive provider of hosted analytics services" alone would also have cured the defect.

Intent is preserved: Section 2.1's no-commitment mechanic and Section 12.3's non-restriction acknowledgment survive without contradiction, the internal conflict created by the original 2.2 is resolved, and no defined term, cross-reference, or commercial mechanic is left dangling. No new Vendor-favourable right or unrelated obligation was introduced.
Tone and comment comply with the playbook: concise first-person-plural explanation of what changed and why, with the narrowed-exclusivity fallback offered without lecturing.
